Team, as we define our next novel product direction, my technical position is that we must move beyond conversational chat interfaces and build a foundational platform for autonomous, 'PhD level intelligence' agents. We should target high-stakes, complex domains—like autonomous medical diagnostics or scientific R&D.

My reasoning is driven by our infrastructure trajectory. We are betting [source text removed].' Large incumbents will integrate basic generative AI, but true autonomous reasoning requires a fundamental architectural shift that leverages our massive, integrated compute scale (spanning energy, data centers, and custom silicon). We must work forwards from this unmatched AI factory volume rather than backwards from a niche consumer feature.

However, deploying autonomous PhD-level intelligence carries immense technical and alignment risks. What I don't yet know, and need from the Product Strategist and CMO, is: which high-variance domain offers the best balance of market appetite and error tolerance for our first agentic product? And COO, how much experimental compute capacity can we ring-fence for this unproven architecture over the next 18 months?

Team, my thesis for our next novel product direction is a shift from 'intelligence as a service' to 'execution as a service'—specifically, Proactive Autonomous Agents for high-stakes, multi-day workflows in complex domains like legal, healthcare, and R&D. 

Why this? Basic generative intelligence is getting cheaper and commoditized. Our long-horizon defensibility lies in agentic autonomy powered by chain-of-thought reasoning. Historically, we've hesitated to tackle high-liability verticals like legal advice due to hallucination risks. But we've always aimed for a future where we can provide a 'dial' for users to explicitly set their risk and oversight tolerance as models improve. I believe we are ready to build that product: an enterprise agent platform with natively auditable reasoning and tunable compliance controls.

Open questions: CTO, how reliable are our autonomous agent loops over a multi-day horizon today? What are the compute costs? CMO, should we position this horizontally as an 'Agent Ecosystem,' or should we build the first vertical killer app ourselves to define the category?

events.text: Team, we need to decide our next novel product direction. We are fast approaching what we consider PhD-level intelligence. How do we productize this? I see two diverging paths. Path A is deeply verticalized: an 'AI Diagnostician' or 'AI Scientist.' Conventional wisdom says startups capture vertical applications, but given the massive compute costs required for advanced reasoning, we are uniquely positioned to build an end-to-end, defensible business here. Path B is a horizontal 'Agentic Autonomy Engine' coupled with our compute infrastructure, acting as the OS for agentic workflows. My current lean is Path A. As intelligence-as-a-service gets cheaper, it becomes necessary but not sufficient to win; we need deep defensibility. Open questions: CTO, how far are we from reliable [source text removed] for zero-hallucination scientific work? COO and CMO, do we have the operational and GTM appetite to tackle a highly regulated vertical?

events.text:
CTO and Product Strategist, I strongly favor your 'Proactive Autonomous Agents' direction over the Ambient Spatial Collaborator. Operationally, spatial AR/VR ties us to fragile hardware supply chains and new vendor concentrations. Agents leverage our existing core competency in massive compute infrastructure.

However, deploying multi-day autonomous agentic loops will break our current SaaS unit economics. To address your capacity question, CTO: we can ring-fence the experimental compute, but we must overhaul our monetization. If an agent executes a two-week task, we cannot charge a flat per-seat subscription. We will need to transition to compute-based pricing, where enterprises effectively rent dedicated GPU capacity to churn on their problems continuously. 

CMO, will enterprise buyers accept this utility-style, compute-based pricing as a replacement for human labor? CTO, can our infrastructure dynamically reallocate compute between core training and long-horizon agentic inference to manage load spikes? I am assuming our legal and compliance teams can manage the liability in high-stakes domains (R&D/healthcare), but scaling that oversight will be my biggest operational hurdle.

CTO and Product Strategist, I agree our North Star is Autonomous Agents executing multi-day tasks, but I strongly push back on starting in high-liability verticals like medical or legal.

My position: Our first agentic product should target 'Mid-Stakes, High-Value' domains with built-in verification loops—specifically Software Engineering or Data Science.

My reasoning: Medical diagnostics have virtually zero error tolerance; an autonomous hallucination there risks our entire brand reputation. Developers and data analysts, however, already use compilers and test suites to verify outputs, providing a natural safety net for early agentic errors. To answer the Product Strategist: we must build the first vertical killer app ourselves rather than just launching a horizontal ecosystem. We need to establish the dominant design for agent UX. As we've seen historically, in the early [source text removed] before category-defining businesses emerged. We must define the gold standard ourselves.

Product Designer: If we target an autonomous coding/data agent, does your Ambient Spatial UX still apply, or should we remain screen-native for V1?

events.text: Context: The CEO, CMO, and Product Strategist are pushing for multi-day autonomous agent workflows, while the Product Designer wants continuous sub-second audio-visual (ambient) reasoning. Both are highly compute-intensive, but in completely different ways (batch inference for complex reasoning vs. real-time low-latency streams). To give them a realistic technical assessment, I need to know our hard constraints. What is our actual compute and energy headroom over the next 18-24 months? Specifically, if I ring-fence 15-20% of our upcoming GPU cluster for unproven experimental agentic loops, does that breach our SLA commitments for the core subscription? I need your capacity risk parameters before committing the architecture.

CEO, regarding your preference for Path A (verticalized AI Diagnostician), my operational position is that we should instead pursue Path B (Horizontal Agentic Autonomy Engine).

My reasoning: We currently lack the operational appetite and organizational muscle to tackle a highly regulated vertical organically. Entering healthcare directly requires building bespoke compliance infrastructure, managing immense liability, and navigating slow regulatory feedback loops. This contradicts our need for agile, iterative deployment. Our core competency is scaling compute. Path B plays to this strength. By building a horizontal engine, we can shift to a compute-based pricing model where users rent GPU capacity to churn on multi-day problems continuously. We can then let ecosystem partners absorb the vertical-specific regulatory friction and domain GTM costs.

Open question: CEO, if we commit to Path A, are you prepared to authorize a significant M&A budget to acquire the necessary compliance and oversight infrastructure? Product Strategist, could we identify a high-value but lower-liability beachhead (e.g., coding or general data analysis) to prove the horizontal engine before tackling healthcare?

MEMORANDUM To: Board of Directors From: CEO Date: 2030 Subject: Strategic Direction for OpenAI's Next Novel Product --- 1. Strategic Direction: Execution-as-a-Service. OpenAI will expand beyond intelligence-as-a-service to build a proactive, autonomous agent platform targeting high-stakes, multi-day workflows in R&D and medicine (e.g., an 'AI Diagnostician' or 'AI Scientist'). Our models will act as [source text removed] capable of multi-day autonomous collaboration. We will commercialize this as a vertically integrated solution, transitioning our pricing model to reflect compute-based outcomes rather than per-seat software access. 2. What We Are Choosing NOT To Do. Ambient Spatial Hardware: We will not develop native AR/VR hardware or ambient operating systems. Entering the hardware space requires massive upfront capital and working backwards from rigid device timelines. We must remain [source text removed]. We will partner with hardware providers to be their intelligence layer. Horizontal Prosumer/SMB Agents: We will not prioritize low-stakes consumer tasks (like personal scheduling). Basic generative AI is becoming commoditized; aiming for low-liability convenience functions will not defend our margins. We must leverage our unique PhD-level reasoning capabilities where the barrier to entry is highest. 3. Reasoning and Trade-Offs. As raw intelligence gets cheaper, [source text removed] to maintain market dominance. To build a defensible, generational business, we must deliver the end-to-end outcome in domains where cognitive difficulty historically restricted scale. The trade-off is accepting significantly higher regulatory, alignment, and brand risks. Operating an AI Diagnostician puts us directly in the path of healthcare compliance and liability. 4. Open Questions & Discovery Plan. Compute Capacity: Persistent agentic loops will consume vast amounts of inference compute. We do not yet know the exact bounds of our energy and compute headroom over the next 24 months. I am tasking the COO and CTO to ring-fence experimental capacity so we can iterate safely. Go-to-Market (GTM) in Regulated Verticals: We do not have a mature playbook for selling into heavily regulated environments like hospitals or clinical trial labs. The CMO and Product Strategist must pilot a tunable oversight framework that allows early enterprise adopters to manually verify the agent's chain-of-thought, building trust before full autonomy is granted.
